66_marg607: Augustine, On the Trinity, book 15. If the charity by which the Father loves the Son, and the Son loves the Father, shows ineffably the union or communion of them both, what is more fitting than that he should be properly called charity who is the Spirit common to both? Otherwise, if in that Trinity the Holy Spirit alone is charity, then the Son is found to be the Son not of the Father alone, but also of the Holy Spirit. For he did not say “of his Son,” which if he said he would say most truly, but he says: “of the Son of his love.” The Son, then, is also the Son of the Holy Spirit, if in that Trinity the charity of God is none other than the Holy Spirit. Since this is most absurd, it remains that the Holy Spirit is not only charity there, but on account of those things of which I have discoursed sufficiently, is properly so called. And as to what is said, “of the Son of his love,” let nothing else be understood than his beloved Son, the Son of his substance. For the charity of the Father is his nature and substance, as we have often said. And therefore the Son of his charity is no other than he who is begotten of his substance.
